pages.title: Rimewood
pages.text: $(italic)Pruinodendron glaciale.$() A squat, wind-shaped conifer with charcoal bark, icy-blue seams and dark teal needles. It keeps growing long after every other tree has died.$(br2)From $(bold)Phase 3$(), small $(bold)groves of two to four$() take root wherever the ground is cold enough, in any land. They are rare and far apart. There are no Rimewood forests.$(br2)$(italic)Rimewood remains metabolically active at temperatures previously classified as incompatible with forestry. ORSA has revised that classification to 'inconvenient.'$()

pages.title: Cultivation
pages.text: Plant a sapling on $(bold)dirt, dead grass or frozen dirt$() with open sky above. It needs no sunlight, but it only grows at $(bold)-20°C or colder$(), so harvesting means working in the cold.$(br2)$(li)About $(bold)25 minutes$() to maturity, or 4-6 bone meal$(li)Warmth pauses growth without harming the sapling; heaters do not help$(li)A tree gives about $(bold)8-12 logs$() and roughly two saplings$(li)Fortune finds more saplings
Each log makes four planks. Rimewood works in every ordinary wood recipe, burns as fuel and smelts to charcoal, and its planks do not freeze.

pages.title: Rimewood Resin
pages.text: Strip a Rimewood log or wood with an axe and the sealed bark gives up one $(bold)Rimewood Resin$(). Each log yields once.$(br2)Resin and sulfur make a $(l:advanced/nether_substitutes)Thermal Binder$(/l), the field stand-in for magma cream.$(br2)Rimewood logs also host $(l:getting_started/frostcap)Frostcap$(/l) on their sides.
